annotations.keyFindings: Eleven of 14 mostly uncontrolled evaluations reported better wellbeing; the two controlled studies found no clear difference.
annotations.limitations: Search ended 2018; high attrition; no pooling.

annotations.keyFindings: Consultation rates were 15 percent lower after referral than in comparison groups (rate ratio 0.85), with larger effects among frequent attenders.
annotations.limitations: Non-randomised comparisons; regression to the mean likely; substantial heterogeneity.

annotations.keyFindings: No clear effect on loneliness (standardised mean difference -0.08); referred activities were often unavailable.
Reported savings came from uncontrolled comparisons and disappeared after adjustment for regression to the mean; community sector costs were rarely counted.
Benefit depends on link worker time, available community activities and readiness; people with complex needs need more contacts and disengage when referred on too quickly.
Eleven reviews drew on 97 primary studies with very high overlap (corrected covered area 18 percent); positive reviews leaned on six small uncontrolled evaluations.
An earlier overview found five low-quality reviews and judged the evidence insufficient for investment decisions.
annotations.limitations: Search ended March 2017; no overlap assessment.

claims.text: A meta-analysis of controlled studies reported consultation rates 15 percent lower after link worker referral, mostly from non-randomised comparisons.
claims.passage: consultation rates at 12 months were 15 percent lower after referral than in comparison groups (rate ratio 0.85, 95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.98)
claims.interpretation: The one pooled service-use benefit rests on non-randomised comparisons prone to regression to the mean.

claims.text: Controlled studies show no clear effect of social prescribing on loneliness.
claims.passage: The pooled effect on loneliness was small and uncertain (standardised mean difference -0.08, 95 percent CI -0.21 to 0.05)
claims.interpretation: Loneliness, a main reason for referral, may not improve on average.

claims.text: Reviews of social prescribing overlap heavily, and positive reviews lean on the same few small uncontrolled evaluations.
claims.passage: the corrected covered area was 18 percent, indicating very high overlap
claims.interpretation: An umbrella review must count primary studies once, or it will repeat the double counting.

claims.text: People with complex needs often need more contacts and disengage when referred on too quickly.
claims.passage: were more likely to disengage when referred onward too quickly
claims.interpretation: Report outcomes for people with complex needs separately where reviews allow.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Reviews of link worker social prescribing report better wellbeing mainly from uncontrolled evaluations, a 15 percent lower consultation rate from non-randomised comparisons, and no clear effect on loneliness. Claimed savings do not survive adjustment for regression to the mean. Reviews overlap heavily, and positive conclusions lean on the same small evaluations. A realist review explains why people with complex needs may benefit less. The one earlier overview is out of date.
gradeRationale: Most reviews rest on uncontrolled or non-randomised primary studies with high overlap between reviews; imprecision for loneliness; certainty that link workers change service use or costs is low to very low.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; one method score out of range and stored as unknown.
